content: Amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP) is a recognized syndrome of shellfish poisoning, primarily associated with the consumption of bivalve mollusks such as mussels, clams, oysters, and scallops. These shellfish are filter feeders, which means they accumulate toxins produced by microscopic algae, specifically dinoflagellates and diatoms. ASP occurs when domoic acid, a neurotoxin, is ingested. In the brain, domoic acid primarily damages the hippocampus and the amygdaloid nucleus. It exerts its toxic effects by activating AMPA and kainate receptors, leading to an influx of calcium into neurons. While calcium influx is a normal cellular process, the excessive and uncontrolled entry of calcium causes neuronal degeneration. Domoic acid can bioaccumulate in marine organisms that consume phytoplankton, such as shellfish, anchovies, and sardines. In mammals, including humans, domoic acid acts as a potent neurotoxin, leading to permanent short-term memory loss, brain damage, and, in severe cases, death. Harmful algal blooms are closely linked to the occurrence of ASP. Importantly, cooking or freezing contaminated fish or shellfish does not reduce the toxicity of domoic acid. The first documented outbreak of ASP occurred in late 1987 in eastern Canada. This outbreak resulted in the deaths of three elderly patients and caused long-term neurological complications in other affected individuals. The syndrome was named amnesic shellfish poisoning due to the prominent symptom of memory loss. The outbreak was traced to cultured mussels harvested from a specific area in Prince Edward Island, which had not previously been associated with toxic algae. Mouse bioassays conducted on extracts from the suspect mussels revealed unusual neurotoxic symptoms distinct from those caused by paralytic shellfish poison or other known toxins. On December 12, 1987, a team of scientists at the National Research Council of Canada began investigating the outbreak. By December 16, they had identified domoic acid as the causative toxin. Domoic acid poisoning has also been implicated in unusual wildlife events. For example, in 2006, a California brown pelican, potentially affected by domoic acid, collided with a car on the Pacific Coast Highway. Additionally, a 1961 incident in Santa Cruz, California, involving thousands of disoriented seabirds may have been caused by domoic acid. This event reportedly inspired Alfred Hitchcock's film The Birds. The clinical presentation of ASP begins with gastrointestinal symptoms, which typically appear within 24 hours of consuming contaminated shellfish. These symptoms include vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and, in some cases, hemorrhagic gastritis. In more severe cases, neurological symptoms develop after a delay of several hours to three days. Treatment for ASP is primarily supportive, as there is no specific antidote for domoic acid toxicity. Patients who have ingested high doses of the toxin or who have risk factors such as advanced age or renal failure are at increased risk of death. Among the 107 confirmed cases in the 1987 outbreak, four fatalities were reported. In some survivors, permanent complications such as short-term memory loss and peripheral polyneuropathy have been documented.
